# Mustang Dies When I Put It in Park

A 1996 Ford Mustang GT dropping below 500 RPM and stalling immediately after engaging Park is a classic symptom of an idle air control system issue, but the timing suggests a specific trigger related to your recent fuel filler repair. In modern engine management systems, particularly those using the OBD-II era architecture common in 1996 vehicles, the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) relies on precise sensor inputs to calculate fuel trim and idle speed. When you shift from Drive to Park, the throttle position sensor (TPS) signal changes, and the PCM expects a corresponding adjustment in airflow managed by the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve or bypass ports. If the engine dies at this specific transition point, the root cause is almost always insufficient air bypass capability when the throttle plate is closed.

The fact that you repaired the fuel filler tube just before this issue emerged provides a critical clue regarding the diagnosis. While it might seem unrelated to the electrical and mechanical idle circuit, a bad fuel leak often forces drivers to check connections tightly or inadvertently disturb adjacent components during reassembly. More importantly, if the repair involved working near the charcoal canister vent line or the purge solenoid, you may have introduced a restriction or a vacuum leak that manifests only under specific conditions. However, there is a more direct mechanical possibility: the act of shifting into Park mechanically locks the transmission. In some older Fords, this engagement can slightly alter the position of the throttle linkage if the cable adjustment is marginal, or it can trigger a vacuum switch logic that expects a certain manifold pressure.

If the PCM detects that the engine speed is dropping too quickly after the shift event, it may interpret this as an open loop failure or a severe vacuum leak and attempt to compensate by flooding the cylinders with fuel. If the compensation overshoots or if the IAC valve is already clogged with carbon buildup from years of operation, the engine simply cannot maintain idle stability. The repair history is significant because disturbing the area around the fuel tank often brings technicians close to the brake booster line or the vacuum reservoir lines that run along the passenger side firewall. A disconnected hose during that job could have gone unnoticed until the car was driven enough for the new leak dynamics to interact with the PCM's idle logic.

To diagnose this without access to a scanner, you can perform a visual and physical inspection of the intake manifold gaskets and the IAC valve housing. Remove the air filter box and locate the small black solenoid mounted on or near the throttle body. Check for vacuum hoses leading directly to the carburetor-style brake booster (on this engine) or the PCV system that might have been pinched off during the filler tube work. If the IAC valve is stuck in a closed position due to carbon accumulation, the PCM cannot maintain idle speed when the transmission engages Park and the load on the drivetrain shifts.

Another potential culprit is the throttle body itself. Over time, varnish from old fuel can coat the bypass ports around the throttle plate. When you shift into Park, the TPS signal tells the PCM to close the throttle slightly, but if the bypass ports are blocked, no air enters the engine. The result is a rapid drop in RPM followed by stalling. Cleaning the IAC valve with a specialized solvent and ensuring all vacuum lines are securely attached to their correct ports is the first line of defense. If the issue persists after cleaning, you may need to check for a sticking throttle cable that prevents the plate from closing fully when the pedal is released, creating a false "wide open throttle" signal that confuses the idle logic.

Since you cannot read codes right now, look for physical signs of vacuum leaks around the intake manifold bolts and the fuel filler neck grommet. A strong hissing sound near the firewall or brake booster line would confirm a leak. If the problem started immediately after the repair, it is highly probable that a hose was not fully seated or a clamp was missed during the reassembly of the filler system. Fixing these mechanical disconnects often resolves electronic stalling issues without needing any software intervention.
